claims.text: The reported HfNbTiVAl10 alloy has a hierarchical heterostructure.
A machine-learning model trained on experimental tensile and fracture data from HfNbTiVAl10 will predict Young’s modulus more accurately than established simulation methods.
The machine-learning model will predict yield strength more accurately than established simulation methods.
The machine-learning model will predict fracture-related behavior more accurately than established simulation methods.
The machine-learning model will make these predictions more rapidly than established simulation methods.
Features of the hierarchical heterostructure govern the alloy’s mechanical response.
Experimental-data-driven machine learning can capture complex nonlinear interactions across multiple length scales in this alloy.
Traditional finite-element or continuum-based simulation methods may overlook some of these multiscale interactions.
Capturing the nonlinear multiscale interactions will improve predictive performance.
Established full-scale finite-element or continuum-based methods are currently used to predict the alloy’s mechanical behavior.
Inadequate representation of hierarchical-microstructure variability in the training data may cause the hypothesis to fail.
Unforeseen deformation mechanisms under non-standard conditions may cause the hypothesis to fail.
The magnitude of the accuracy and efficiency improvement depends on the quality and representativeness of the experimental training data.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis predicts improvements in both accuracy and speed, whereas the falsification rule ambiguously combines accuracy and efficiency with “or” and only requires performance in a majority of tests. It therefore does not clearly falsify the hypothesis when one of the two promised gains fails.
